Recorded inclusive; the exclusive reading would place the end when the following day begins. Actor: the order itself. No later amending event is held.

Terminated by its own terms at the close of Saturday, July 4, 1959, the last day section 2 mentions: it limits the section 1 excusal for national-security employees and employees who work or are excused on Saturday, July 4, 1959, so it has no force once those days passed. Recorded inclusive; the exclusive reading would place the end when the following day begins. Actor: the order itself. No later amending event is held.

Terminated by its own terms at the end of fiscal year 1960, June 30, 1960: section 3 gives an employee not excused on July 3, 1959 one other workday off in fiscal year 1960 at a time the employee requests and the agency approves. The date June 30, 1960 comes from the fiscal-year definition (statutory, not a held text); no held source shows the leave date extended or the grant cancelled earlier. Recorded inclusive; the exclusive reading would place the end when the following day begins. Actor: the order itself. No later amending event is held.

research_rationale:
Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing of Executive Order 10825 (24 FR 4825, PDF pages 1-3; Federal Register issue of June 13, 1959; govinfo PDF text layer held at jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_10825.txt), headed Executive Order 10825, signed by Dwight D. Eisenhower on June 12, 1959. The census register gives the same number, date and subject (Excusing Federal Employees From Duty All Day on July 3, 1959). The text is an official scan read through its machine text layer; I read it for OCR damage and note below where damage matters. Inventory: section 1(a) excuses covered employees from duty all day on Friday, July 3, 1959 (with section 1(b) giving a rule for employees whose workday spans two calendar days); section 2 limits the excusal for national-security employees and employees working or excused on Saturday, July 4, 1959; section 3 gives employees who are not excused on July 3, 1959 one other workday off in fiscal year 1960; section 4 denies any basis for holiday, premium or overtime pay for July 3, 1959 and requests agency heads to arrange their affairs for the excusal. Inventory correction: the dossier's second clause (subsection (b)) runs from section 1 across a Register page break and then through the Contents and unrelated Register documents. The order is split by a page break (continued on next page), and the last sentence of section 4 is badly damaged in the text layer; I use five spans: section 1, section 2, section 3, the first part of section 4, and the surviving fragment of the end of section 4. The recitals are not operative and are not clauses. The damaged fragment is read against the American Presidency Project transcription (not quoted, and not cited as a source), which shows that the last sentence of section 4 requests agency heads to arrange their affairs so that employees can be excused from duty on that day or given compensatory time, without additional appropriations. Own terms: sections 1, 2 and 4 are tied to July 3 and 4, 1959; section 3 runs to the end of fiscal year 1960, which is June 30, 1960 (the Government's fiscal year ran from July 1 to June 30; that statutory definition is not a held text and the order does not state the date, so I disclose that the end of section 3 rests on it). The whole order therefore ends on June 30, 1960. The three chosen machine searches (U.S. Code through 2026-10-09, eCFR as of 2026-10-14, Office of the Federal Register disposition notes plus operative sentences of 17521 saved order texts) each state their coverage with no warning; their coverage notes were read. They search by this order's number, and none returned a hit for it.

savings.reason: The order contains no savings, exception or transitional clause beyond the limits in section 2 and the pay denial in section 4, which restrict the excusal and do not continue it. Pay and leave for the excused day and for the alternate workday rest on the leave statutes and are completed effects.
